newsitem.title: USA: Alaska governor signs bill limiting civil awards.
newsitem.headline: Alaska governor signs bill limiting civil awards.

text.p: A bill that limits monetary awards in Alaska civil cases was signed on Friday by Gov. Tony Knowles, to the applause of business representatives and the criticism of consumer advocates.
"I'm here to sign a bill that is important to keep Alaska's business climate healthy while protecting the rights of injured Alaskans," Knowles, a Democrat, said at a signing ceremony.
He said the bill "represents a careful compromise that really took two years to reach."

Championed by the legislature's Republican majority, the new law limits punitive damages to $500,000 or three times compensatory damages. In aggravated cases, the punitive award is capped at $7 million or four times the amount of financial gain that resulted from the defendant's misconduct.

It limits compensatory awards for non-economic damages to the greater of $400,000 or $8,000 per year of the plaintiff's life expectancy. In aggravated cases, the limit is $1 million or $25,000 per year of the plaintiff's life expectancy.
The bill also allocates half of punitive awards to the state treasury.
The bill supplanted one with lower caps and more restrictions on plaintiffs that passed the legislature last year but was vetoed by Knowles.
After the veto, Knowles appointed a task force to study reform issues. It discovered that civil awards in Alaska tended to be small and punitive awards were rare.
That information led some panel members to conclude that tort reform was unnecessary, Thomas Stewart, a retired state judge who chaired the committee said.

Stewart said he was one of those who was sceptical about the need for the law -- and disagreed with the provisions that placed absolute limits on civil awards -- but added that the bill that passed was much better than the bill that Knowles had vetoed last year.
The executive director of an Alaska consumer-rights organisation promised a court fight to challenge the bill.

Steve Conn, head of the Alaska Public Citizens Research Group, said the bill's award caps, limits on childrens' abilities to recover awards and wrongful-discharge provisions were among those that could be unconstitutional.
He blamed corporations for spreading the "myth" that limits are needed on civil awards. "The public is not going to be fooled forever on this stuff," he said.
National consumer advocate Ralph Nadar this week fired off a letter to Knowles describing the governor's support of the bill as "deplorable."
